correctness.rationale: The real-part equation has exactly one real root by strict monotonicity. All other zeros are in a bijection with the distinct eligible real roots of P(x)=8x³−2(2b−a)x+1, each contributing exactly two conjugate zeros. The cubic discriminant is 64[4(2b−a)³−27]. In b>a, the negative root always satisfies x<−sqrt((b−a)/3), while eligibility of the positive roots follows from their relation to the critical point sqrt((2b−a)/12) and the exact sign P(sqrt((b−a)/3))=−sign E. The proof distinguishes all folds and axis collisions and treats multiple roots only once. For (a,b)=(3,5/2), P=(2x−1)(4x²+2x−1) and J=2y²P′(x)≠0 at each nonreal root; the sole real root has positive Jacobian. The actual embedded standard-library verifier was executed and passed exact witness and transition checks plus 20,000 independent finite sampled comparisons; the analytic reduction, not finite computation, proves the universal statement.

value.rationale: Carlson studies parameter-dependent zero counts of the exact family in separated asymptotic regimes, and Brooks et al. explicitly discuss extending the diagonal case to unequal coefficients. This proof completely classifies the natural first nontrivial cubic/linear case for every a,b>0, including sharp values at fold and real-axis collision loci; it distinguishes two phase-boundary mechanisms and exhibits an open off-diagonal seven-regular-zero region. This is substantive structural completeness, rather than an arbitrary numerical slice, a known diagonal recomputation, or a routine asymptotic strengthening.
